judgments.reasoning_cat1: The consent is to transfer "Your information" in a corporate transaction and to use it "for any purpose allowed under this Agreement" — a broad but internally bounded formula; the opening sentence is descriptive rather than operative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The linked privacy policy (Section 5) may impose narrower limits, but nothing in the four corners contradicts this consent, and Section 31 expressly carries it forward. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The initial term is not stated but left to "Your membership Plan," and the refund trigger — termination "merely ... for its convenience" where "You are not in breach" — turns on an undefined characterisation that Angie's List itself controls. "[F]or any reason in its sole discretion" alongside a conditional refund invites two readings of when a refund is owed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with Section 6's automatic-renewal and cancellation terms (c008, c014) and with c013's statement that refunds apply "only to downgrades, not to cancellations"; the survival list in Section 31 (c047) also omits Section 18 while purporting to be non-exhaustive.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A unilateral right to "modify and restate" the whole agreement, effective "immediately upon being posted," coupled with deemed consent from continued use, is the classic clause whose enforceability and scope are argued over; "You will receive notice" is not tied to any method or timing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Immediate effectiveness on posting sits against Section 28 (c043), under which notices are deemed delivered only on verification or two business days after sending, and against the preamble's promise of notice of modifications (c001). Those two timing rules cannot both govern a posted modification.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[G]eneral practices, policies and limits, which may or may not be published" is unbounded and unknowable to the member, and the enumerated examples are introduced by "including without limitation," leaving the catch-all's reach uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A right to "limit access to, modify, change or discontinue the Service" without liability is difficult to square with the specific paid Plan benefits promised in Section 1 and with the pro rata refund in Section 18 (c027), though the disclaimers in Sections 24 and 25 pull the same way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[L]imitations, delays and other problems inherent in the use of the Internet" is vague at the edges — "inherent" does the whole work of the disclaimer — but the provision is short and its target is obvious.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the more general disclaimers in Sections 20, 24 and 25 without contradicting them. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Submissions" is defined to include "other information" sent to Angie's List, which is far wider than the creative ideas the paragraph is about, and the provision purports to vest property in material sent contrary to an express request.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12 (c021) states that Angie's List "does not claim ownership of any of the reviews, ratings, communications, information, data, text or other materials You give us," while this section makes Submissions "the property of Angie's List" — a direct contradiction over overlapping categories of user material.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The carve-out ("Aside from user-submitted Content and Service Provider Content") is clear and the defined term "Copyright Materials" is closed by an enumerated list with a standard "including, but not limited to."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits with Sections 9, 12 and 22 and is expressly preserved by Section 31. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The first sentence is garbled — "NO RESPONSIBILITY OR LIABILITY FOR THE TIMELINESS, DELETION OF CONTENT OR FAILURE BY THE SERVICE" leaves "timeliness" and "failure by the Service" without a coherent object — and the closing carve-out for jurisdictions that forbid implied-warranty disclaimers leaves it uncertain which disclaimers survive where.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The "as is" disclaimer pulls directly against the affirmative description of the Service in the preamble and Section 1 (c001, c002) and against the specific Plan benefits sold in Section 1; a court reconciling those would have real work to do.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It lists nearly every damages category — including "DIRECT" and "COMPENSATORY" — under the collective defined term "DAMAGES," and then adds catch-alls ("ANY OTHER MATTER RELATING TO THE SERVICE") whose reach against the enumerated items is uncertain; the closing jurisdictional carve-out leaves the survivor set unstated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A blanket exclusion of all liability for "ANY BREACH OF THIS AGREEMENT BY ANGIE'S LIST" cannot be reconciled with the cap in the next paragraph (c035), which presupposes liability up to one month of fees, or with c036's statement that "ANGIE'S LIST SHALL BE SOLELY LIABLE FOR THE PAYMENT OF ANY DAMAGES TO YOU."

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cap formula is arithmetically specific (one month, or the prorated monthly value), and the recital about "unlimited access ... represents a substantial portion of the value" is a justification rather than an operative term of uncertain meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes recoverable liability that c034 has just excluded outright, and its recital that unlimited access is a substantial portion of the value sits against Sections 20 and 24, which permit Angie's List to limit or discontinue access without liability — a recital-versus-operative tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The parenthetical "(AS DEFINED HEREIN AND SUBJECT TO THE LIMITATIONS SET FORTH IN THIS SECTION SUFFERED BY YOU" is never closed, so it is unclear where the qualification ends and the operative release begins — a mechanical error that changes what is released.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its final sentence — Angie's List "SHALL BE SOLELY LIABLE FOR THE PAYMENT OF ANY DAMAGES TO YOU UNDER THIS AGREEMENT" — contradicts c034's exclusion of all liability for breach, and the "Released Parties" defined here are made third-party beneficiaries by Section 32 (c048).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The indemnified group includes Angie's List's "users," which is a startlingly broad class in a member agreement, and trigger (c) — "any intentional or willful violation of any rights of another or harm You may have caused to another" — is open-ended; "Angie's List will have sole control of the defense" also sits oddly with an obligation on the member to defend.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The member's unlimited indemnity is asymmetric with the one-month cap on Angie's List's liability (c035), which is a one-sidedness point rather than a contradiction; c036's separate indemnity of the Released Parties overlaps.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The trigger is "if it becomes necessary for Angie's List to pursue legal action to enforce the terms" — it is unclear whether liquidated damages accrue on breach or only on suit, and the recited premise that "damages are often difficult to calculate" is a conclusion rather than a standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its premise of incalculable damages is contradicted by subsection (d) (c042), which requires payment of "actual damages ... to the extent such actual damages can be reasonably calculated" — the recital and the operative fallback point in different directions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[E]ach item of Content posted in violation of this Agreement" leaves the counting unit undefined (a review? a sentence? a photograph?), and the sentence "We may (but shall not be required to) to issue You a warning" contains a duplicated "to."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Whether "Content posted in violation" refers to the Section 16 conduct warranties or to Section 12 is not specified, and subsection (d) purports to reserve actual damages for everything outside (a)-(c) using lettering that does not match this subsection's own label.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The per-item $1,000 charge again depends on the undefined unit "each item of Content," the verb list ends with the catch-all "exploit for any purpose," and the subsection ends without a full stop.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It substantially overlaps c039 — a single act could be both posting and exploiting Content — and it is referenced by subsection (d) as "(b)," a labelling mismatch running through Section 27.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[E]ach review or record that is aggregated, disrupted, damaged or otherwise affected by You" is an open-ended measure — "otherwise affected" following specific harms is a classic catch-all of uncertain reach — and multiplied by $100 it can produce wildly different totals on different readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It tracks Section 16(G)-(H) (c025) but uses different language ("aggregate records or reviews"), so the conduct covered by the liquidated sum and the conduct prohibited do not map exactly onto each other.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It excepts "the foregoing subsections (a) through (c)" when the foregoing subsections are labelled (A), (B) and (C), and it conditions actual damages on their being "reasonably calculated" — a standard the section's own premise denies is achievable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: "Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement" overrides the rest of the instrument on remedies, sitting against the Section 30 forum clause and the remedies already reserved in Section 16; and it contradicts the incalculability premise in c038.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[D]eemed delivered upon the earlier of the verification of delivery or two (2) business days after being sent" is unusual — "earlier" rather than "later" — and notice by "posting the notices on the Website" has no identifiable date of sending to run the two days from.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 19 (c028) makes modifications effective "immediately upon being posted," which cannot be squared with this deemed-delivery rule, and the cancellation channels in c014 (including a different street-address formulation) are not aligned with the notice addresses here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The procedure is a near-verbatim statutory checklist, but it repeatedly extends the DMCA — a copyright statute — to "trademark" claims, which is a mismatch between the authority invoked and the rights covered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supplements the general notice provision in the same section without contradicting it, and Section 23 (c032) supplies the proprietary-rights backdrop. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It is an integration clause without any no-reliance language, and it is limited to agreements "regarding the subject matter contained in this Agreement" — a qualifier that requires a court to decide what subject matter the Agreement actually covers before the clause can do any work.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The preamble (c001) requires acceptance of terms "in, and linked to, this Membership Agreement" and contemplates separate terms for other Angie's List sites, and Section 5 points to an external privacy policy — so the "entire agreement" is on its face not entire.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It selects "exclusive jurisdiction" in Marion County, Indiana and then, in the same sentence, permits Angie's List alone to elect another forum — "exclusive" and the unilateral election cannot both be literally true, and the one-sidedness is the sort a court construes against the drafter. The one-year limitations bar for any claim "arising out or related to" use of the Service is also missing a word and broad in scope.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Indiana choice of law and the shortened limitations period run against consumer-protection rights the Agreement nowhere addresses, and the section must be read with Section 27(d)'s "[n]otwithstanding any other provision" remedies reservation (c042); the internal exclusivity conflict is within this clause rather than across the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[I]ncluding, but not limited to, Sections 12, 14, 15, 17 and 23 through 31" is the textbook general-versus-specific problem: an express enumeration coupled with a non-exhaustive preface, so the survival of unlisted sections is genuinely uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The list omits Section 13 (c022), which contains a broad liability disclaimer, and stops at 31, excluding Section 32 (c048) with its severability and third-party-beneficiary terms — yet those provisions plainly need to survive, so the enumeration and the rest of the instrument do not fit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The severability sentence is drafted as an instruction that a court "should incorporate a similar provision that would be considered valid," which is an unusual and indeterminate reformation direction rather than a standard blue-pencil rule.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It makes the "Released Parties" — a term defined only in Section 25 (c036) — third-party beneficiaries, so the two must be read together; Section 31 (c047) does not list Section 32 among the surviving provisions, which sits awkwardly with a severability and beneficiary clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short assent-and-acknowledgment statement in plain, unconditional terms; there is nothing in it whose meaning could be disputed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It repeats the acceptance language of the preamble (c001) — assent by use rather than by clicking — which raises formation questions but does not contradict any operative term. No conflict found.
